clinicalPearls: Irritant contact dermatitis is the commonest form, sparing the inguinal and gluteal skin folds because the convex surfaces in contact with the napkin bear the brunt of friction, moisture and irritants.
Fold involvement is the key clue that the picture is no longer simple irritant dermatitis and points to candidal infection, seborrhoeic dermatitis, or intertrigo.
Candidal napkin dermatitis characteristically shows beefy-red confluent erythema with peripheral scaling and satellite papules and pustules extending into the folds.
Prolonged skin wetness raises pH and activates faecal proteases and lipases, so the mainstay of prevention is frequent changing, gentle cleansing and a barrier preparation.
Jacquet erosive dermatitis is a severe irritant form with punched-out ulcers and raised papulonodules, seen with chronic diarrhoea or infrequent changing.
A napkin eruption that is erosive, purpuric, ulcerated or unresponsive to standard care should raise suspicion of Langerhans cell histiocytosis, zinc deficiency or child neglect.
Perianal streptococcal disease and staphylococcal folliculitis can mimic or complicate napkin dermatitis and should be considered with a well-demarcated painful perianal erythema.
Low-potency topical corticosteroid for short courses helps inflammatory cases, but potent fluorinated steroids under occlusion of the napkin risk atrophy and granuloma gluteale infantum.
reference.pathophysiology: Napkin dermatitis is predominantly an irritant contact dermatitis arising from the occluded, humid microenvironment beneath a nappy. Sustained contact with urine and faeces increases skin hydration and surface pH, which in turn activates faecal proteolytic and lipolytic enzymes that degrade the stratum corneum barrier. Friction against the napkin, maceration and repeated wetting-drying cycles compound the barrier disruption, allowing irritants and microbes to penetrate. Overgrowth of Candida albicans from the gastrointestinal tract frequently supervenes on damaged skin, and secondary bacterial colonisation may occur. Underlying inflammatory dermatoses such as seborrhoeic dermatitis, atopic eczema and psoriasis can localise to or be exacerbated within the napkin area because of the Koebner phenomenon and occlusion.
additionalDifferentials: seborrhoeic dermatitis involving the folds and scalp
atopic dermatitis with secondary napkin involvement
acrodermatitis enteropathica or acquired zinc deficiency
perianal streptococcal dermatitis or bullous impetigo
additionalInvestigations: skin swab and microscopy or culture for Candida when folds are involved or satellite lesions present
bacterial swab for suspected streptococcal or staphylococcal secondary infection
serum zinc and alkaline phosphatase if an acrodermatitis-like periorificial and acral eruption coexists
skin biopsy for persistent, erosive or petechial eruptions to exclude histiocytosis
stool assessment when chronic diarrhoea is driving an erosive irritant pattern
blood glucose and immune screen where recurrent or refractory candidiasis suggests underlying immunodeficiency
patch testing in older children with suspected allergic contact dermatitis to wipes or fragrances
redFlags: erosive, ulcerated or purpuric lesions suggesting Langerhans cell histiocytosis rather than simple irritant rash
periorificial and acral dermatitis with diarrhoea and alopecia indicating zinc deficiency
failure to respond to appropriate barrier and antifungal treatment
systemic upset, spreading cellulitis or blistering suggesting invasive bacterial infection
features raising concern for neglect such as a severe untreated eruption with poor general care
reference.prognosis: Simple irritant napkin dermatitis resolves rapidly with barrier protection and improved hygiene and clears completely once nappies are discontinued. Recurrence is common while in nappies, and persistent or atypical eruptions require reassessment for an alternative underlying diagnosis.
pitfalls: treating fold-involving candidal dermatitis as pure irritant rash and omitting an antifungal
prescribing potent fluorinated corticosteroids under napkin occlusion, causing atrophy or granuloma gluteale infantum
missing acrodermatitis enteropathica by not examining periorificial and acral sites
overlooking Langerhans cell histiocytosis in an erosive, petechial or treatment-resistant eruption
attributing all perianal erythema to irritation and missing perianal streptococcal disease
